slides.title: Form A: item 1
slides.html:
On a construction sheet, two angles carry the same arc mark, but one is drawn much wider than the other. The sheet says matching arc marks are givens. What can you conclude? What should be fixed in the drawing?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The angles are congruent because the stipulated marks are givens. The inaccurate rendering should be corrected; the drawing does not cancel an explicit hypothesis. No numerical angle measure follows without a degree label.

Reveal second check

Erase the picture and retain the written equal-mark convention: congruence still follows, while a numerical value remains undetermined.

slides.title: Form A: item 2
slides.html:
Someone claims f(n) = n² + n + 41 gives a prime for every whole number n. (A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.) Work out f(40) exactly. Is the claim true?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

f(40)=1600+40+41=1681=41². Thus 41 is a positive divisor other than 1 or 1681, so the value is not prime. The single input 40 refutes the universal conjecture, regardless of how many smaller cases worked.

Reveal second check

Factor directly: 40²+40+41=40·41+41=41(40+1)=41². This factorization independently checks the decimal arithmetic.

slides.title: Form A: item 3
slides.html:
Lines l and m are different and cross at P. Q is on l but is not P. R is on m but is not P. Can the line through Q and R also go through P? Use only facts about which points lie on which lines.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. If QR passed through P, uniqueness for P, Q would make it l. It would then contain P, R, so uniqueness for P, R would make it m. This forces l=m, a contradiction.

Reveal second check

In the valid configuration, the three connecting lines PQ, PR, QR form a triangle of incidences, not three lines through P. No angle or length theorem is used.

slides.title: Form A: item 4
slides.html:
A made-up round planet has a circumference of 43,200 km. Two sites on one north-south circle are 900 km apart along the surface. If every degree of center angle matches the same arc length, what is the center angle? Name one assumption you would need to say this equals a shadow angle.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Angle=360·900/43,200=7.5 degrees. Identifying it with a shadow angle additionally requires the specified meridian arrangement and parallel sunlight, together with the later parallel-angle justification. That identification is a preview assumption, not proved here.

Reveal second check

The recovered fraction 7.5/360=1/48 equals 900/43,200.

slides.title: Form A: item 5
slides.html:
A pen moves from A = (0, 0) to B = (4, 0) to C = (4, 3) to D = (0, 3) and stops. Is this path a polygon yet? Which single straight segment would finish a simple four-sided polygon?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The trace is open, so it is not a polygon boundary. Add DA. This joins the remaining endpoint D to A without crossing the other edges and closes the four-sided chain.

Reveal second check

The initial trace has endpoints A, D of degree 1; after adding DA, each of the four vertices has two incident boundary edges.

slides.title: Form A: item 6
slides.html:
A circle centered at M and a circle centered at N have the same radius r. They share the point X. The distance MN is not given. Which of MX, NX and MN must equal r? Use only definitions.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

MX=NX=r because X lies on both circles. MN need not equal r: equal radii do not specify the distance between centers. No congruence theorem is needed.

Reveal second check

Choose centers distance r apart for one model and 1.5r apart for another; both allow overlapping equal-radius circles, but the center distances differ. Only the stated circle incidences force the radius equalities.

slides.title: Form A: item 7
slides.html:
A made-up system has four points and only two lines: {A, B} and {C, D}. Its one rule is 'every point is on exactly one line.' Does the system follow the rule? Does the rule force all the points onto one line?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Yes, the listed model satisfies the axiom because each point appears in exactly one listed line. No, it does not force one common line; this very model is a counterexample. This is a toy system, not a claim that its finite lines satisfy Euclidean axioms.

Reveal second check

Count line memberships: A, B, C, D each have 1. Neither of the two line sets contains all four points.

slides.title: Form A: item 8
slides.html:
A bin holds two compasses, C1 and C2, and one straightedge, S. All three are metal. For this bin, decide whether each claim is true: 'every compass is metal' and 'every metal object is a compass.' For a false claim, name an object that shows it.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The first is true on this stated finite bin: C1, C2 are metal. The second is false because S is metal but is a straightedge, not a compass. The claims are converse implications, not equivalent definitions.

Reveal second check

Exhaust the 3 listed objects. S has Metal=true, Compass=false, the exact truth pattern falsifying Metal⇒Compass.

slides.title: Form A: item 9
slides.html:
A 'triad' means three different points that are not all on one line. A proposed test is 'the record lists three point names.' Give two different records that pass the test but are not triads. Then write an exact 'if and only if' test.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

A record A, A, B has repeated points; A, B, C with three collinear locations has distinct names but still fails. A record is a triad iff it names exactly three distinct points and no single line contains all three.

Reveal second check

A noncollinear triangle passes the repaired test. Each false positive fails a different required condition, so both conditions are needed.

slides.title: Form A: item 10
slides.html:
You are given a = b + c and b = d + e. Prove a = d + e + c. A classmate writes c = d + e instead. Which statement follows, and why?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Substitute b=d+e into a=b+c: a=(d+e)+c=d+e+c. Nothing identifies c with b, so c=d+e does not follow.

Reveal second check

Counterexample to the extra assertion: d=1, e=2, c=4, b=3, a=7 satisfies both givens but c≠3. The proved equation gives 7=1+2+4.

slides.title: Form A: item 11
slides.html:
Use only these two rules: x < x is never true, and if x < y and y < z, then x < z. Prove that a < b and b < a can't both be true.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Assume both. Transitivity gives a<a, contradicting irreflexivity. Hence the two inequalities cannot both hold. The rules are explicit premises of this logic task, not an appeal to a later inequality lesson.

Reveal second check

The same substitution with roles reversed also gives b<b. Either violates the first printed rule.

slides.title: Form A: item 12
slides.html:
A system has three assumptions. S: every marked point is on line l. T: point P is marked. U: P is not on l. Can all three be true together? Show that removing any one of them gets rid of this contradiction.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Together S and T put P on l, contradicting U. Delete U: put marked P on l. Delete T: put unmarked P off l and use no marked points. Delete S: put marked P off l. Thus all three assumptions together are inconsistent, and every two-assumption subset has a model.

Reveal second check

Use two Boolean facts M=(P marked), L=(P on l). The assumptions are M⇒L, M, not L. Their conjunction is false in all four truth rows; each two-assumption subset has a satisfying row.

geo.title: Form A: item 12
geo.prompt: A system has three assumptions. S: every marked point is on line l. T: point P is marked. U: P is not on l. Can all three be true together? Show that removing any one of them gets rid of this contradiction.
geo.solution: Together S and T put P on l, contradicting U. Delete U: put marked P on l. Delete T: put unmarked P off l and use no marked points. Delete S: put marked P off l. Thus all three assumptions together are inconsistent, and every two-assumption subset has a model.
geo.check: Use two Boolean facts M=(P marked), L=(P on l). The assumptions are M⇒L, M, not L. Their conjunction is false in all four truth rows; each two-assumption subset has a satisfying row.

slides.title: Form B: item 1
slides.html:
A circle has two chords that look equal, with no marks. Eli writes 'the chords are congruent because the picture is symmetric.' What information, if it were given, would make that a fair given? What is still unproved in the drawing as it is?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

An explicit chord-equality mark or a written equality could supply that equality as a given. As drawn, neither congruence nor an exact symmetry was specified or proved. Merely looking symmetric is insufficient.

Reveal second check

Move one chord’s endpoint along the same circle while preserving the stated circle incidence; the chord lengths can differ. This retains every actual hypothesis.

slides.title: Form B: item 2
slides.html:
A sequence starts at u0 = 2, and each term is the one before plus 3: u(n + 1) = u(n) + 3 for every whole number n. Find u3. Why is this deduction and not a guess from a pattern?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The rule gives u1=5, u2=8, u3=11. Each step follows an explicitly supplied rule, so it is deductive. A bare list 2, 5, 8 without the rule would not establish a unique continuation.

Reveal second check

Reverse each step by subtracting 3: 11→8→5→2. The given universal recurrence, not a visual pattern, licenses those steps.

slides.title: Form B: item 3
slides.html:
Four survey markers are all different, and no three of them are on one line. A report says only five lines are needed to connect every pair of markers. Show the report is wrong without measuring any angles.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

There are 6 unordered pairs. If two different pairs determined the same full line, their union would contain at least 3 distinct collinear markers, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus all 6 lines are distinct; five is impossible.

Reveal second check

List AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD. The no-three-collinear condition prevents every possible collapse of two pair-lines.

slides.title: Form B: item 4
slides.html:
On one round-planet model, a 9 degree north-south arc is 1,000 km long. On another it is 1,500 km. Using the same 'equal arc for each degree' rule, which planet is bigger around, and what is the ratio?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Both arcs are 9/360=1/40 of a full circle. Circumferences are 40,000 and 60,000 km, so the second is larger with ratio 3: 2. This is arithmetic within the given spherical models, not an unproved general similarity theorem.

Reveal second check

60,000/40,000=1,500/1,000=3/2. Multiplying each circumference by 1/40 returns its own given arc.

slides.title: Form B: item 5
slides.html:
A simple five-sided region has B and D on its boundary. Point W lies between B and D but outside the region; these facts are given. Is the region convex? Which part of the definition fails?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

It is not convex. Both endpoints B, D belong to the region, but their joining segment contains W outside it. This directly violates the requirement that every such joining segment stay in the region.

Reveal second check

The statement “every joining segment stays inside” is refuted by the single witness segment BD and its point W. No distance, slope or triangle-angle theorem is needed.

slides.title: Form B: item 6
slides.html:
Circle c has center P and passes through Q, where P and Q are different. Circle d has center Q and passes through P. The two radii are equal. Are c and d the same circle? Decide by checking whether P is on each one.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. P belongs to d because d was drawn through P. P does not belong to c: its distance from c’s center P is 0, less than the positive radius PQ. Thus one set contains a point the other does not.

Reveal second check

Q supplies the opposite witness: Q is in c but not in d. Equal radius does not imply identical centers or identical circles.

slides.title: Form B: item 7
slides.html:
A system's only assumptions are 'A implies B' and 'B implies C.' Show that A implies C. Must 'C implies A' also follow? Give true or false values for A, B and C to back up your answer.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

If A holds, the first rule gives B and the second gives C, so A⇒C. The reverse need not hold: A=false, B=false, C=true makes both assumptions true but C⇒A false.

Reveal second check

Evaluate the counterassignment directly: F⇒F and F⇒T are true, whereas T⇒F is false.

slides.title: Form B: item 8
slides.html:
A device rule says 'if the switch is on, then the lamp is on.' Four observations of (switch, lamp) are (off, off), (off, on), (on, on) and (on, off). Which one breaks the rule? Does seeing the lamp on prove the switch is on?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Only (on, off) violates the implication. An on lamp does not certify an on switch because (off, on) is explicitly observed and does not violate the contract.

Reveal second check

Map switch/lamp to(P, Q). The violating row is(T, F); the reverse inference is refuted by(F, T).

slides.title: Form B: item 9
slides.html:
A database calls a pair of real numbers (x, y) 'reciprocal.' Its test is x + y = 1. Find a pair that passes the test but shouldn't, a pair that fails but should pass, and the correct exact test.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

False positive: (2, -1) has sum 1 but product -2. False negative: (2, 1/2) has product 1 but sum 2.5. Correct test: xy=1, which also forces both entries nonzero.

Reveal second check

Compute the two products and sums independently. If xy=1, then y=1/x and x=1/y; conversely either reciprocal relation gives product 1.

slides.title: Form B: item 10
slides.html:
Solve x² = x for real numbers. A classmate divides both sides by x right away and gets only x = 1. Find every solution and the case that was lost.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Move terms: x²-x=x(x-1)=0. The zero-product rule gives x=0 or x=1. Division by x assumes x≠0 and loses the valid solution 0.

Reveal second check

Substitution gives 0²=0 and 1²=1. For x not 0 or 1, neither factor is zero, so there is no additional solution.

slides.title: Form B: item 11
slides.html:
You are given two rules: 'H implies E' and 'H implies not E.' Prove 'not H' by contradiction. Don't assume E or not E before you start.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Assume H. The first rule derives E, and the second derives not E. The contradiction E and not E rejects H, so not H. Both branches are necessary to expose the contradiction.

Reveal second check

In a truth table, any row with H=true makes at least one of the two given implications false. All rows satisfying both have H=false.

slides.title: Form B: item 12
slides.html:
System U assumes exactly one line through every two distinct points. System E assumes at least one line through every two distinct points and does not assume uniqueness. (In plain words: For every pair of different points, U requires exactly one line through both points. E requires at least one line through both points, but allows either one or more than one.) Does 'two different lines can't share two different points' hold in both systems? If not, build a small example that breaks it.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

It follows in U by uniqueness. It need not follow in E: take points P, Q, R, S and line-sets l={P, Q, R}, m={P, Q, S}, n={R, S}. Every point pair has at least one listed line, but distinct l, m both contain P, Q. This is a toy incidence countermodel, not a Euclidean plane.

Reveal second check

List six pairs: PQ lies on l, m; PR, QR on l; PS, QS on m; RS on n. All existential requirements hold while uniqueness fails.

slides.title: Exit ticket
slides.html: 1. What's confusing?
